Antiandrogen medications may lead to the development of gynecomastia. 3. Patients with known or previously unrecognized candidiasis may experience more pronounced symptoms during therapy, necessitating treatment with an antifungal agent. 4. Metronidazole injection contains 790 mg of sodium per 100 mL. Exercise caution when administering this injection to patients on a controlled sodium diet, those taking corticosteroids, or individuals predisposed to edema. 5. Severe neurological disturbances, including encephalopathy, cerebellar symptoms, convulsive seizures, and aseptic meningitis, have been reported in patients treated with metronidazole. Patients should be advised to report any neurological symptoms that occur during treatment. Discontinue metronidazole if abnormal neurological symptoms such as ataxia, dizziness, confusion, or other central nervous system adverse reactions occur. 6. Cases of severe hepatotoxicity or acute hepatic failure, including fatal outcomes with rapid onset after treatment initiation, have been reported in patients with Cockayne syndrome using systemic metronidazole. In this population, metronidazole should only be used after a careful benefit-risk assessment and if no alternative treatment is available. 7. Liver function tests should be obtained prior to starting therapy, within the first 2-3 days after initiation, frequently during therapy, and after treatment ends. Discontinue metronidazole if liver function test elevations occur, and monitor until baseline values are restored. 8. Patients with Cockayne syndrome should stop taking metronidazole immediately if they experience symptoms of potential liver injury, such as abdominal pain, nausea, changes in stool color, or jaundice, and contact their healthcare provider. 9. When prescribing metronidazole tablets for bacterial infections, patients should be instructed to take the medication exactly as directed. Skipping doses or not completing the full course of therapy may reduce the effectiveness of treatment and increase the likelihood of bacterial resistance, making future infections harder to treat. 10. Hypersensitivity reactions, including severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs), can occur and may be life-threatening. 11. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies of metronidazole use in pregnant women. Some studies, including those with first-trimester exposure, have suggested an increased risk of cleft lip, with or without cleft palate, in infants exposed to metronidazole in utero, though these findings were not confirmed. 12. Metronidazole crosses the placental barrier, and its effects on human fetal organogenesis are unknown. 13. Metronidazole is present in human milk at concentrations similar to maternal serum levels, and infant serum levels can approach therapeutic levels. There is no data on the effects of metronidazole on milk production. 14. Due to potential carcinogenicity observed in animal studies, a decision should be made to discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug, considering the importance of the drug to the mother. 15. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for therapy and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed infant from the drug or the underlying maternal condition. 16. Nursing mothers may choose to pump and discard breast milk during metronidazole therapy and for 24 hours after therapy ends, feeding their infant stored human milk or formula. 17. Metronidazole inhibits nucleic acid synthesis by disrupting DNA and causing strand breakage, exhibiting amebicidal, bactericidal, and trichomonacidal properties. 18. Protein binding of metronidazole is less than 20%. 19. Metronidazole undergoes side-chain oxidation, resulting in two metabolites: 1-(β-hydroxyethyl)-2-hydroxymethyl-5-nitroimidazole and 2-methyl-5-nitroimidazole-1-ylacetic acid. 20. The drug is cleared with a half-life of approximately 10 hours when administered orally. 21. Some drugs may be incompatible with reconstituted solutions containing metronidazole HCl but compatible with ready-to-use IV solutions containing metronidazole, and vice versa. 22. Additives such as aztreonam and cefepime may be used, but further dilution in glass or plastic containers to no more than 8 mg/mL with normal saline, D5W, or lactated Ringer’s solution is recommended. 23. Neutralize the solution with approximately 5 mEq of sodium bicarbonate per 500 mg of metronidazole to achieve a final pH of 6-7. No dilution or buffering is necessary for ready-to-use IV solutions. 24. Metronidazole should only be administered via infusion. Avoid contact between the drug and aluminum in the infusion set, though this is less critical for ready-to-use infusion solutions containing metronidazole rather than metronidazole HCl. 25. Vaginal metronidazole is an antibiotic commonly used to treat bacterial vaginosis caused by specific bacteria. However, its appropriateness depends on the causative organisms, as resistance may reduce its effectiveness. 26. Vaginal metronidazole may also be used for other conditions as determined by a healthcare provider. 27. Vaginal metronidazole is available as a 0.75% vaginal gel under brand names such as Nuvessa and Vandazole, as well as generic forms. 28. Store vaginal metronidazole at room temperature (68°F to 77°F or 20°C to 25°C). It can tolerate short-term exposure to temperatures between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C) during transport. 29. Common side effects of vaginal metronidazole include headache, vaginal itching, stomach pain, nausea, painful or heavy periods, sore throat, rash, diarrhea, breast pain (with Vandazole), and vaginal yeast infections. 30. Vaginal yeast infections may occur during or after treatment with vaginal metronidazole, which does not treat yeast infections. Signs of a yeast infection include vaginal discharge, itching, or discomfort, and may require antifungal treatment. 31. Serious side effects of vaginal metronidazole include severe allergic reactions (e.g., breathing problems, swelling, hives, dizziness, or joint pain) and nervous system problems (e.g., seizures, peripheral neuropathy, confusion, or behavioral changes). 32. Patients allergic to metronidazole, Nuvessa, Vandazole, parabens, nitroimidazole derivatives, or any ingredients in the product should not use vaginal metronidazole. 33. Vaginal metronidazole should not be used with certain medications, such as warfarin, disulfiram (within the past two weeks), or lithium. 34. Avoid alcohol or foods containing alcohol or propylene glycol while using vaginal metronidazole and for at least one day after stopping Nuvessa or three days after stopping Vandazole. 35. If an overdose occurs, seek immediate medical attention, call 911, or contact a Poison Control Center. 36. If a dose is missed, use it as soon as remembered unless it is close to the next dose. Do not double doses. Complete the full prescribed course to reduce the risk of resistance. 37. Vaginal metronidazole is for vaginal use only. If it contacts the eyes, rinse with cool water and contact a healthcare provider. 38. Inform your healthcare provider of all health conditions and medications, including nervous system disorders, before using vaginal metronidazole. 39. Discuss pregnancy and breastfeeding plans with your healthcare provider, as metronidazole passes into breast milk and its effects on pregnancy are not fully known.
